metadata.description: General pet care including vaccinations, dental care, grooming, exercise, parasite prevention, and wellness

entries.title: Core Vaccination Schedule for Dogs
entries.content: Vaccinations are one of the most important preventive health measures for dogs and have saved millions of lives by preventing serious and often fatal infectious diseases. Core vaccines are recommended for all dogs regardless of lifestyle. The DHPP combination vaccine protects against Distemper which attacks the nervous system and is often fatal, Hepatitis from adenovirus, Parvovirus which is a severe gastrointestinal disease with high mortality especially in puppies, and Parainfluenza one component of the kennel cough complex. Rabies vaccine is required by law in most US states and is always a core vaccine. Puppy vaccination schedule: 6-8 weeks give the first DHPP, at 10-12 weeks give the second DHPP, at 14-16 weeks give the third DHPP and the first rabies vaccine. Then booster DHPP at 1 year after the puppy series. After that, DHPP is typically boosted every 1-3 years depending on the type of vaccine and your veterinarian's protocol. Rabies is boosted at 1 year after the first vaccine and then every 1-3 years depending on local laws and vaccine type. Non-core vaccines are recommended based on lifestyle and geographic risk and include Bordetella for kennel cough highly recommended for dogs who board, attend daycare, or visit dog parks, Lyme disease for dogs in tick-endemic areas, Leptospirosis for dogs with outdoor water and wildlife exposure, and Canine influenza. Discuss your dog's specific lifestyle with your veterinarian to create the appropriate vaccine protocol.
entries.when_to_see_vet: Annual or biannual wellness exams to keep vaccinations current and assess overall health

entries.title: Core Vaccination Schedule for Cats
entries.content: Cat vaccinations protect against serious diseases that remain prevalent in the feline population. Core vaccines are recommended for all cats regardless of whether they live indoors or outdoors. The FVRCP combination vaccine also called the feline distemper vaccine protects against Feline Viral Rhinotracheitis which is caused by herpesvirus and causes upper respiratory infections, Calicivirus which causes upper respiratory disease and oral ulcers, and Panleukopenia which is feline distemper, a severe and often fatal gastrointestinal and immune disease. Rabies vaccine is required by law in most states even for indoor cats since bats can enter homes and there is potential for human exposure. Kitten vaccination schedule: 6-8 weeks give the first FVRCP, at 10-12 weeks give the second FVRCP, at 14-16 weeks give the third FVRCP and first rabies vaccine. Booster FVRCP at 1 year after the kitten series. After that, FVRCP is typically boosted every 1-3 years. Non-core feline vaccines are recommended based on lifestyle risk and include Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) vaccine which is highly recommended for outdoor cats or cats with exposure to other cats since FeLV is transmitted by close contact and causes serious immune suppression and cancer. FeLV vaccine is recommended as core for all kittens by many veterinary organizations. Feline Immunodeficiency Virus (FIV) vaccine efficacy is debated and has testing interference issues so consult your vet. Indoor cats still benefit from rabies and FVRCP vaccines since respiratory viruses can be carried in on clothing.
entries.when_to_see_vet: Annual or biannual wellness exams to keep feline vaccinations current

entries.title: Dental Care for Dogs and Cats — A Complete Guide
entries.content: Dental disease is the most common disease in companion animals with studies showing that 80% of dogs and 70% of cats over age 3 have some degree of periodontal disease. Dental disease is not just bad breath — it causes significant oral pain, tooth loss, and bacteria entering the bloodstream can damage the heart, kidneys, and liver. Signs of dental problems include bad breath (halitosis), yellow or brown tartar buildup on teeth, red or inflamed gums (gingivitis), pawing at the mouth, dropping food, drooling, swollen face, and reluctance to eat hard food. Home dental care: tooth brushing is the gold standard. Use pet-specific toothpaste in flavors like poultry or seafood since human toothpaste contains fluoride and xylitol which are toxic to pets. Use a soft-bristled pet toothbrush or a finger brush. Start by letting the pet lick the toothpaste off your finger, then progress to touching gums, then finally to actual brushing. Even 30 seconds of brushing a few times per week is beneficial. Dental chews and water additives approved by the Veterinary Oral Health Council (VOHC) can supplement brushing but do not replace it. Professional dental cleanings under anesthesia are necessary when tartar buildup is significant and to properly probe for pockets below the gum line where disease begins. Annual dental examinations and cleanings every 1-3 years depending on the individual pet are recommended. Do not give hard objects like bones, antlers, or hard nylon toys that can fracture teeth.
entries.when_to_see_vet: Annual dental examination; professional cleaning every 1-3 years under anesthesia depending on severity

entries.title: Pet Grooming Guidelines by Coat Type
entries.content: Regular grooming keeps pets comfortable, prevents skin problems, and is a valuable opportunity to check for lumps, wounds, parasites, and other health concerns. Short-coated breeds such as Beagles, Boxers, and Siamese cats need minimal grooming. Weekly brushing with a rubber curry brush or grooming mitt removes dead hair, distributes natural oils, and stimulates the skin. Bathing every 4-8 weeks or as needed. Double-coated breeds such as Huskies, German Shepherds, Labrador Retrievers, and Maine Coon cats shed heavily and need brushing 2-3 times per week with an undercoat rake or shedding blade especially during seasonal coat blows in spring and fall. Never shave double-coated breeds as the coat provides insulation from both heat and cold. Long-coated breeds such as Afghan Hounds, Maltese, Persians, and Ragdoll cats require daily brushing to prevent painful matting. Mats pull skin, trap moisture, and harbor parasites. Professional grooming every 6-8 weeks is recommended. Curly or wavy coated breeds such as Poodles, Doodles, Bichon Frises, and Devon Rex cats require regular professional grooming every 6-8 weeks since their coats continue growing and mat easily. Nail trimming should be done every 4-6 weeks for most pets. Ear cleaning is needed for floppy-eared breeds every 2-4 weeks to prevent infections. Introduce grooming gradually to puppies and kittens with positive reinforcement to build lifelong tolerance.
entries.when_to_see_vet: If skin abnormalities, masses, or ear problems are found during grooming

entries.title: Exercise Requirements for Dogs by Breed Size and Type
entries.content: Adequate exercise is fundamental to a dog's physical health, mental wellbeing, and behavioral stability. Insufficient exercise is a leading cause of destructive behavior, excessive barking, and hyperactivity. Exercise needs vary enormously by breed size, breed type, and age. Small breeds such as Chihuahuas, Shih Tzus, and French Bulldogs generally need 30 minutes to 1 hour of daily activity split into 2 walks plus play sessions. Note that Brachycephalic breeds (Bulldogs, Pugs, Boston Terriers) overheat easily and should not exercise in hot weather or with high intensity. Medium breeds such as Cocker Spaniels and Bulldogs need about 30-60 minutes daily. Large breeds such as Labrador Retrievers and Golden Retrievers need 1-2 hours of active exercise per day including walking, fetching, and swimming. Working and herding breeds such as Border Collies, Australian Shepherds, Huskies, Belgian Malinois, and Vizslas need 2 or more hours of vigorous activity and significant mental stimulation daily. These high-drive breeds are frequently rehomed due to owners underestimating their needs. Senior dogs need gentler, shorter exercise with rest breaks but still benefit greatly from daily walks for joint health, weight management, and mental stimulation. Puppies should follow the 5-minute rule: 5 minutes of exercise per month of age twice daily to protect developing joints from over-exercise. Mental exercise through training, puzzle toys, and sniff walks can be as tiring as physical exercise and should be incorporated daily.
entries.when_to_see_vet: Consult vet before significantly increasing exercise in senior or overweight pets

entries.title: Parasite Prevention — Fleas, Ticks, and Heartworm
entries.content: Year-round parasite prevention is one of the most important aspects of routine pet care and significantly impacts both pet and human health since some parasites are zoonotic meaning they can affect people. Fleas are the most common external parasite. A single flea can lay 50 eggs per day making infestations difficult to eliminate. Fleas cause flea allergy dermatitis, transmit tapeworms, and can cause severe anemia in small animals. Prevention requires treating all pets in the household simultaneously and treating the environment since 95% of the flea population lives in carpets, bedding, and furniture rather than on the pet. Effective products include monthly oral or topical preventatives such as Nexgard, Simparica, Bravecto, Revolution, and Frontline Gold. Ticks transmit serious diseases including Lyme disease, Ehrlichia, Anaplasmosis, and Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever. Check pets after outdoor activities especially in wooded or grassy areas. Remove ticks promptly with fine-tipped tweezers grasping close to the skin surface. Tick preventatives should be used in any geographic area with tick exposure. Heartworm disease is transmitted by mosquitoes and is potentially fatal requiring extensive treatment in dogs and having no safe approved treatment in cats. Heartworm prevention such as Heartgard, Interceptor, or Revolution should be given year-round or at minimum seasonally in all dogs and cats based on veterinary recommendation. Annual heartworm testing in dogs is required before or alongside starting prevention. Intestinal parasites including roundworms, hookworms, whipworms, and giardia are diagnosed by annual fecal testing and treated with appropriate dewormers.
entries.when_to_see_vet: Annual fecal testing, heartworm testing in dogs, and parasite prevention prescription from your vet

entries.title: Senior Pet Care Guide for Dogs and Cats 7 Years and Older
entries.content: Senior pets have unique health needs that require more attentive monitoring and more frequent veterinary care than young adults. Dogs are generally considered senior at 7 years for small and medium breeds and as early as 5-6 years for large and giant breeds since large breeds age faster. Cats are generally considered senior at 10-11 years. Common health changes in senior pets include: reduced mobility and joint pain from arthritis which affects 80% of dogs over age 8, cognitive dysfunction syndrome (CDS) in dogs similar to dementia with symptoms of disorientation, altered sleep patterns, and house soiling, hyperthyroidism in cats, kidney disease which is the leading cause of death in senior cats, dental disease, heart disease, and cancer with the risk increasing significantly with age. Senior wellness care recommendations: increase veterinary exams to every 6 months from the annual visit since conditions can change rapidly at this age. Annual bloodwork including complete blood count and chemistry panel, urinalysis, and blood pressure measurement to catch organ changes early when treatment is most effective. Maintain regular gentle exercise to preserve muscle mass and joint health. Provide orthopedic bedding, ramps instead of stairs for arthritic pets, raised food bowls, and easy litter box access. Senior diets formulated for the specific condition may be beneficial. Pain management for arthritis dramatically improves quality of life and is frequently underutilized. Monitor for lumps and bumps monthly since cancer risk increases significantly with age.
entries.when_to_see_vet: Every 6 months for senior pets; annual bloodwork and urinalysis are essential

entries.title: Benefits of Spay and Neuter Surgery
entries.content: Spaying which is the removal of ovaries and uterus in females and neutering which is the removal of testicles in males are routine surgical procedures performed under general anesthesia with significant health and behavioral benefits. Health benefits of spaying: eliminates the risk of pyometra which is a life-threatening uterine infection affecting up to 25% of intact females, eliminates uterine and ovarian cancer risk, dramatically reduces mammary tumor risk especially when spayed before the first heat cycle. Females spayed before the first heat have less than 0.5% risk of mammary cancer compared to 26% in intact females. Health benefits of neutering: eliminates testicular cancer which is common in intact males, significantly reduces prostate disease risk, and eliminates certain hormone-driven behaviors. Behavioral benefits: reduces roaming and escape attempts driven by the urge to find a mate, may reduce aggression in some cases particularly fighting between intact males, eliminates heat cycles in females which occur every 6 months in dogs and seasonally to continuously in cats. Timing of surgery: traditionally recommended at 6 months but recent research especially in large breed dogs suggests waiting until 12-18 months for better musculoskeletal development. Discuss optimal timing for your specific pet and breed with your veterinarian. Benefits to the community include reducing pet overpopulation and the euthanasia of millions of animals in shelters annually. Most spay and neuter procedures are routine and safe with rapid recovery in healthy young animals.
entries.when_to_see_vet: Discuss optimal timing for your individual pet's breed, size, and sex with your veterinarian

entries.title: Microchipping Your Pet — Permanent Identification
entries.content: A microchip is a small radio-frequency identification transponder about the size of a grain of rice that is implanted under the skin between the shoulder blades using a needle similar in size to a vaccine needle. The procedure is quick, requires no anesthesia, and causes minimal discomfort similar to a routine vaccine. Each microchip has a unique 15-digit ISO standard number that is linked to the owner's contact information in a microchip registry database. When a lost pet is scanned at a veterinary clinic or shelter, the chip number is read and the owner's contact information is retrieved from the registry. Microchips are not GPS devices and do not track location but they do provide permanent proof of ownership that cannot be removed like a collar or tag can. Studies show that microchipped dogs are returned to their owners at a rate of 52% compared to 22% for non-chipped dogs. For cats, microchipped cats are 20 times more likely to be reunited with their owners. After getting your pet microchipped it is essential to register the chip number in a searchable database such as the AAHA Universal Pet Microchip Lookup and keep your contact information current whenever you move or change phone numbers. Check that the chip is still readable at annual vet exams since chips can occasionally migrate. Even with a microchip, keep current ID tags on your pet's collar at all times for immediate identification by anyone who finds them.
entries.when_to_see_vet: Can be done at any routine vet visit or during spay/neuter surgery under anesthesia

entries.title: Annual Pet Wellness Exam Checklist and What to Expect
entries.content: Annual wellness exams are the cornerstone of preventive veterinary care and allow early detection of health problems before they become serious and costly. Even if your pet appears healthy, many conditions have no outward signs in early stages. What happens during a wellness exam: nose-to-tail physical examination including listening to the heart and lungs, palpating the abdomen for organ size and lumps, checking lymph nodes, examining eyes, ears, and mouth, assessing skin and coat, and evaluating body condition score and weight. Vaccination review and administration of any boosters that are due based on your pet's protocol. Fecal examination to check for intestinal parasites from a fresh stool sample brought from home. Heartworm test for dogs which is a simple blood test. Bloodwork discussion including whether baseline blood testing or more comprehensive panels are indicated based on age, breed, and health history. Parasite prevention products prescription or review of current prevention protocol. Dental examination to assess tartar and gum health and determine if a professional cleaning is needed. Nutrition counseling including review of current diet and any needed adjustments. Discussion of any behavioral concerns or changes noticed at home. Questions you should bring to the appointment: any changes in eating, drinking, urination, defecation, activity level, weight, behavior, and any new lumps or bumps. Senior pets should have exams every 6 months. Bringing a list of all medications and supplements helps the veterinarian provide complete care.
entries.when_to_see_vet: Annual for adults 1-7 years; biannual (every 6 months) for puppies, kittens, and seniors
